_comment: Expectations, stated separately from the input in osv-records.json.
These were produced by a second implementation of the same OSV rules,
written in Python from the schema rather than from the Go code, and spot
checked by hand. Two independent readings of the same bytes have to agree.
A fixture that computes its expectation with the code under test proves
only that the code agrees with itself.
parse: what reading one record whole must produce. severity is the three
step chain - the database's own word, then a CVSS v3 vector, then the
records this one is an alias of. An empty string means the feed genuinely
publishes no severity anywhere, which is true of 19 of these 267 records.
CVSS v4 is deliberately not scored: its base score is a lookup table, not a
formula, and inventing a number is worse than admitting we have none.
match: what the range walk must answer at the versions golden-register is
actually on. One finding exists across the whole workspace and it is
GO-2026-5932 on golang.org/x/crypto. 39 packages are not-found: the feed
carries no record for them at all, which is NOT the same claim as clean and
is exactly the distinction every index file used to lose.
probes: for each record, one version its own published range covers, and the
package it belongs to. A record commonly carries several maintenance branches
fix that applies depends on which branch you are on. So the expectation is
stated against a named version rather than the record as a whole.
severitySource names which step of the chain answered: word, cvss, alias,
or empty when the feed publishes no severity anywhere. Stating it here is
what lets a test prove the cvss step earns its place instead of matching on
the shape of pretty printed JSON, which is how it went unguarded.
errors: the status codes and bodies the API really produces, and what each
must become. Note that a package the feed has never heard of answers 200
with the body {} - byte identical to a package with no vulnerabilities.

errors.why: 200 with an empty body is the feed saying it has never heard of this package. It is also what a clean package returns, which is why the outcome is recorded rather than inferred.
nothing was measured. Recording zero vulnerabilities here is the bug that made 56 index files claim packages were clean.
a record named by a package query and then missing is a broken feed, not a clean package. It fails rather than warning.

counts.why: 92.9 percent of records resolve to a severity. Reading only the database's own word covers 56 percent; the CVSS vector and the alias hop are what carry the rest.
